title: Work-efficient parallel approximate flow
formal:
Does undirected vertex-capacitated maximum flow admit a uniform randomized parallel \((1+\varepsilon)\)-approximation with nearly-linear total work and polylogarithmic depth?

Given an undirected graph with \(n\) vertices and \(m\) edges, distinct terminals \(s,t\), and nonnegative vertex capacities, the algorithm must output a feasible \(s\)-to-\(t\) flow of value at least \(\mathrm{OPT}/(1+\varepsilon)\), where \(\mathrm{OPT}\) is the maximum feasible flow value. It must use \((n+m)\operatorname{polylog}n\) work (total processor operations) and \(\operatorname{polylog}n\) depth (parallel steps), with success probability at least \(2/3\).

The polynomially bounded capacities, inverse-polylogarithmic accuracy regime, uniformity and word-PRAM model are quantified below.

source_formulation.text: The vertex-capacitated maximum-flow part of the source asks for a parallel approximation algorithm with nearly-linear total work and polylogarithmic depth.
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of the vertex-capacitated branch of FOCS 2025 §III, Open Problem 1 (Open Problem 8.1 in the full version). The card selects this single problem.

why: A small depth bound makes an algorithm useful on many processors only when the total work also remains close to input size. Vertex capacities model bottlenecks shared by all routes through a location. The question asks whether such bottlenecks admit the same efficient parallel approximation as ordinary undirected edge-capacitated maximum flow.
status_note: FOCS 2025 explicitly poses this vertex-capacitated maximum-flow target. The source’s general algorithm has subpolynomial overhead instead of the requested polylogarithmic factors. The previous bounded status review through 16 September 2026 found no matching resolution; this wording change on 6 November selects one problem and does not constitute a new exhaustive status review.

progress.text: Published work establishes nearly-linear work and polylogarithmic depth for approximate undirected edge-capacitated maximum flow.
FOCS gives a general parallel flow algorithm with subpolynomial overhead and explicitly asks for nearly-linear work with polylogarithmic depth for vertex-capacitated maximum flow.
ICALP publishes a polylogarithmic-depth result for the restricted unit-data expander setting, with a bicriteria guarantee.

sentences: The question concerns parallel approximation of maximum flow in undirected graphs with vertex capacities.
Each vertex limits the total traffic through it, and the algorithm must explicitly output a feasible flow between the two named terminals.
The flow value must be within a factor of one plus the requested inverse-polylogarithmic error of optimum.
The target combines nearly-linear total processor work with polylogarithmic parallel depth.
The ordinary edge-capacitated version has such an algorithm; this card asks only for the vertex-capacitated version.

definitions:
An input graph \(G=(V,E)\) is finite, simple and undirected, with \(V=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), \(n\ge2\), \(m=|E|\), and distinct named terminals \(s,t\). It is supplied by an explicit edge list; disconnected graphs and zero capacities are allowed. For each undirected edge \(\{u,v\}\), a flow has nonnegative values \(f_{uv},f_{vu}\). Put
\[
\mathrm{out}_f(v)=\sum_{w:\{v,w\}\in E}f_{vw},\qquad
\mathrm{in}_f(v)=\sum_{w:\{v,w\}\in E}f_{wv}.
\]
Require \(\mathrm{in}_f(s)=\mathrm{out}_f(t)=0\) and \(\mathrm{in}_f(v)=\mathrm{out}_f(v)\) for \(v\notin\{s,t\}\). The value is \(F=\mathrm{out}_f(s)=\mathrm{in}_f(t)\). Fractional flows are allowed. Internal circulations may occur but consume vertex capacities.

Each \(v\) has capacity \(U_v\ge0\). Its load is \(\mathrm{out}_f(v)\) if \(v\ne t\), and \(\mathrm{in}_f(t)\) if \(v=t\). Require load at most \(U_v\) for every vertex, including both terminals. Edges impose no additional capacity bounds; only the vertex loads constrain feasibility. Equivalently, in a decomposition into directed simple terminal paths, every unit uses capacity at each vertex on its path, including its endpoints; removable internal circulations do not improve the optimum.

\(\mathrm{OPT}\) is the maximum \(F\) over feasible real flows. Zero flow is feasible, and instances with \(\mathrm{OPT}=0\) must also be handled. The output explicitly lists rational values for both orientations of every edge. On a successful run all feasibility inequalities hold exactly and \(F\ge\mathrm{OPT}/(1+\varepsilon)\); no vertex-capacity violation is permitted.

Here is an explicit polynomial-data and inverse-polylogarithmic-accuracy convention. For every fixed integer \(a\ge1\), allow integral vertex capacities \(U_v\in[0,n^a]\). Let
\[
L=\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil,\qquad
\varepsilon=1/q,\quad q\in\mathbb N,\quad 2\le q\le L^a.
\]
Input numbers, labels and \(q\) are encoded in binary. The same algorithm must cover every fixed \(a\); it receives the numerical instance and \(q\), not advice or a precomputed structure for the graph. Reciprocal-integer accuracies specify the source's inverse-polylogarithmic regime: intermediate accuracies can be met by requesting a smaller reciprocal accuracy. This does not require a fully polynomial bound for arbitrary inverse accuracy outside that regime.

Use a synchronous priority-CRCW word PRAM: processors execute one fixed finite program, have labelled shared-memory words, can read concurrently, and simultaneous writes to one location retain the value of the lowest-numbered writing processor. A step performs word arithmetic, comparison, a Boolean operation, a shift, a shared-memory access, or generation of one independent fair random bit. A word has \(C_a L\) bits for a fixed constant \(C_a\); larger integers and rational numerators or denominators use multiple words and their operations are charged accordingly. There is no exact-real or arbitrary-precision unit-cost primitive. Work counts all processor operations, including input handling and output; depth is the number of synchronous steps. The algorithm must halt within the stated bounds on every random tape and succeed with probability at least \(2/3\) on each valid input.

Nearly-linear work and polylogarithmic depth mean that, for every fixed \(a\), there are constants \(K_a>0\) and \(k_a\in\mathbb N\), independent of the graph, its numerical data and \(q\), such that
\[
\mathrm{work}\le K_a(n+m)L^{k_a},\qquad
\mathrm{depth}\le K_a L^{k_a}.
\]
These are explicit editorial model conventions for the source's parallel resource question. They count the finite precision needed by an actual implementation. Polynomially many processors without the work bound, or a subpolynomial factor that is not bounded by a fixed power of \(L\), is insufficient.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of this existence assertion for undirected vertex-capacitated maximum flow. A positive answer must specify one uniform algorithm and establish exact capacity feasibility, the approximation guarantee, per-instance success probability and simultaneous work/depth bounds for every fixed data-and-accuracy exponent \(a\). A negative answer must rule out such an algorithm in the stated model. The question is binary; there is no additional numerical \(1/100\) tolerance. A theorem about the optimum value alone must also supply the required flow output, and a capacity-violating bicriteria result alone does not meet the stated feasibility guarantee.

context_blocks.text: A vertex capacity bounds the total traffic passing through that vertex, including traffic using different incident edges. In this card both terminals also have capacities, so every unit of flow consumes capacity at every vertex on its path.
The source obtains subpolynomial parallel overhead for a broader flow problem. Its Open Problem 1, numbered 8.1 in the full version, includes the vertex-capacitated maximum-flow target selected here.

This is a single-commodity problem: there is just one source and one sink. The source also studies multiple terminal demands, whose dependence on the number of commodities is outside this card’s target.
SODA 2024 gives an undirected edge-capacitated maximum-flow approximation using work O(m ε^{-3} polylog n) and depth O(ε^{-3} polylog n). That result does not impose vertex capacities.

The ICALP 2026 result concerns unit capacities and unit lengths on expanders. For conductance φ it gives work near m/(εφ) and depth near 1/(εφ), with approximate congestion and cost while routing prescribed demand exactly. Its restricted graph class and bicriteria guarantee leave the general question here unresolved.

The SPAA 2025 exact-flow algorithm has square-root, rather than polylogarithmic, depth. Its near m+n^{3/2} work is nearly linear on sufficiently dense instances; this does not supply the simultaneous bounds sought for all graphs.
